prompt: A sleep app company recruits $300$ VOLUNTEERS and randomly assigns half to use the app and half to a placebo app. App users fall asleep significantly faster. What conclusion is justified?

choices.label: The app causes faster sleep for all adults, since the result was significant
The app caused faster sleep for these volunteers, but the result cannot be generalized to all adults
There is only an association, because volunteers were used
No conclusion is possible without a random sample

hint: Two separate questions: Can we claim CAUSE? Can we GENERALIZE? Each depends on a different kind of randomness.

hints.text: Two separate questions: Can we claim CAUSE? Can we GENERALIZE? Each depends on a different kind of randomness.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: random ASSIGNMENT lets you say "the treatment caused it." Random SELECTION lets you say "and that holds for the whole population." Check which one this study has.
Treatments were randomly assigned (yes to cause). Subjects were volunteers, not a random sample of adults (no to generalizing).
Cause for these volunteers, but no generalization: choice B.

explanation: Random assignment balances everything else between the two groups, so a significant difference can be attributed to the app: a causal claim is justified for the subjects studied.
The subjects were volunteers, not randomly selected from all adults. Volunteers for a sleep study may differ from everyone else, so the result should not be extended to all adults.
Choice B captures both halves. Choice C ignores the random assignment; choice D ignores that experiments can still show cause without a random sample.

alternativeExplanations.title: The two-by-two scope table
steps: Random assignment + random selection: cause, and generalize.
Random assignment only (this study): cause, for these subjects.
Random selection only: association, generalizable. Neither: association, for these subjects.

alternativeExplanations.title: The trap in choice A
steps: "Significant" means the difference is unlikely to be due to chance in the random assignment.
It says nothing about who the subjects represent.
Statistical significance never substitutes for random selection.
